claim: Splitting a task into stable sub-assemblies cuts expected search or build time by orders of magnitude, but only when each part can be finished and checked on its own (Simon's watchmakers: about 4,000 times; ten dials: about 500 tries against 100^10). This is an analytic result, not an experiment.
agent_test: Build two task sets, one with clean independent sub-parts and one with tightly chained parts. Compare O3-on versus plain at equal tokens; predict gain only on the first set.
audit_note: Simon's Hora and Tempus (about 4,000 times, 1/111 x 20 x 20,000) and ten-dial safe (100^10, about 10 x 50 = 500 tries with clicks) match the original; Ulrich (1995) defines modular vs integral architecture and does not corroborate the numbers, so the quantitative claim rests on Simon alone (an analytic parable, as the claim says).

claim: How you cut matters as much as whether you cut: splitting by hidden design decision beats splitting by processing step on change cost and parallel work (one toy system, argued not measured).
agent_test: Give the agent two prompts for a multi-file coding task: split by step versus split by decision. Then apply a change request and count files touched and tests broken, at equal tokens.

claim: A controlled vocabulary for function (verb plus flow object) was reached by two efforts that overlapped heavily (46 and 47 of 53 function terms shared), but the overlap was never shown to improve designs. Both efforts drew on the same older literature.
agent_test: Low priority. If tried: constrain sub-problem statements to verb-object form and compare plan quality against free text at equal tokens.

claim: Different people derive the same function model more often when using the structured derivation method (repeatability). Participant numbers and agreement figures were not read.
agent_test: Run the agent 5 times on the same product description with and without a fixed vocabulary; measure agreement of sub-function sets between runs.

claim: In human studies, evidence that a functional decomposition step improves ideas or design quality is absent: a first controlled test (Linsey et al. 2005) reported no difference from a control group, a within-subject comparison of three decomposition methods (Booth 2013, 26 students) found no method effect on its measures, and an observational study of 78 industry reports (Booth 2015 study 2) found no correlation between using decomposition and design grade (r=0.075, p=0.515). All tests are small, observational or preliminary, so a small benefit is not excluded.
agent_test: Run O3 as a compulsory first step versus none on open design-style tasks, scored by code-checkable constraints, at equal tokens. Expect no gain on open tasks and use that as the null to beat.
audit_note: Booth 2013 (26 students, n=78 trees, no method effect) and Booth 2015 study 2 (n=78, r=0.075, p=0.515) match, but Booth 2013 compares three decomposition methods with each other and measures functions, errors and abstraction levels, not idea count or design quality against a no-decomposition control; Booth 2015 study 2 is observational; the Linsey 2005 figures (n=54, 19.0 vs 19.7) could not be opened (ASEE page blocked; only an abstract saying function modelling was indistinguishable from control was reachable) and the quoted evidence line itself lists group sizes of 5 and 7.
claim_before_audit: In human studies, adding a functional decomposition step shows no reliable benefit for idea count or design quality: Linsey 2005 (n=54, 19.0 vs 19.7 ideas), Booth 2013 (n=26, all four hypotheses rejected), Booth 2015 study 2 (n=78, r=0.075, p=0.515). All tests are small, observational or preliminary, so a small benefit is not excluded.

claim: Which decomposition method is used changes what is listed more than what is built: top-down gave the most functions (19.7 vs 15.1 for enumeration), energy-flow the most final features (8.8 vs 5.0). Cells hold 4 to 16 teams; the function-table counts (11, 13, 16) do not sum to the 25 teams, and the energy-flow feature cell is only 4 teams.
agent_test: Compare top-down versus free listing of sub-problems on coverage of a hidden checklist of required sub-problems, at equal tokens.

claim: The function list tends to fix the design space: nearly all final features map to listed functions (unmapped features 0.0 top-down, 0.2 enumeration, 1.3 energy-flow), and the no-function control produced more highly novel concepts (5 vs 2 scoring 4 or more). The authors give three readings the data cannot separate. An unopened 2016 report says a function tree caused no more fixation than control, and a 20-novice abstract reports more novelty with function terms as stimuli. Update (gap search): Atilola 2015 thesis (N=61) shows a function tree of an example gave no fixation versus control and less than a sketch, but sketch plus tree together was worst (omnibus p=0.083, pairwise p=0.036 to 0.043); this concerns a shown decomposition, not the designer's own.
agent_test: On open-answer tasks, measure diversity of final answers with and without a sub-problem list shown before generation. Also test whether decomposing after a first free attempt avoids the narrowing.

claim: Novices misuse the method: they confuse parts with functions, miss flows, and stop at a general level. In the industry sample 51% of function diagrams were rated very low quality, with a mean of 5.88 syntax errors per diagram. The authors rated quality themselves, so a null may reflect poor use, not a poor method.
agent_test: Score LLM sub-problem lists for parts-versus-functions confusion (a sub-problem that names a solution instead of a need). Add a code check that rejects solution-naming sub-problems and compare.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-27 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Sub-functions from a standard vocabulary need not match easily solvable sub-problems (a cup needs 12 basis sub-functions; some basis functions are hard for a new technology), so decomposition should stop where a solution exists. ADaPT shows the same in LLM agents: decompose only when the executor fails, and deeper tasks need deeper splits.
agent_test: Compare up-front full decomposition versus failure-triggered decomposition (O3 fired only at impasse, as G1 requires) at equal tokens on deep and shallow tasks.
audit_note: ADaPT numbers (71.6/43.3, depth 2 and 3) and Vermaas cup/twelve-subfunction and electrical-to-rotational examples match; 'decomposition should stop where a solution exists' is the researcher's inference, and ADaPT's rule is to decompose only on executor failure.

claim: Failure-triggered recursive decomposition beat up-front plan-and-execute with GPT-3.5 (ALFWorld 71.6 vs 43.3; TextCraft 52.0 vs 27.0; WebShop 44.0 vs 17.0). Under the Yao executor on the ALFWorld test split the gap is smaller (79.8 vs 63.4 plan-and-execute, 67.2 Reflexion; retry-only 56.7). Extra calls are not cost-matched.
agent_test: Re-run on a current model with a retry baseline given the same call budget.

claim: Decomposition helps more on longer problems in least-to-most (GSM8K 5+ steps 45.23 vs 39.07 for chain of thought) and in decomposed prompting (kth-letter concatenation stays near 100% while chain of thought falls with length), and was worse on 2-step GSM8K (74.53 vs 76.68); ADaPT still lifts TextCraft at depth 3 (ReAct 1.8 to 38.7) though its absolute gain is smaller than at depth 2 (26.9 to 78.2).
agent_test: In the S0 gate, route by expected step count. Compare always-decompose versus route-by-length at equal tokens on a mixed-length set. Predict always-decompose loses on short items.
audit_note: GSM8K step-wise numbers, TextCraft depth 2 and 3 numbers and the kth-letter result all match, but the TextCraft numbers cited do not show a gain growing with depth: the absolute ADaPT gain shrinks from +51.3 points at depth 2 (26.9 to 78.2) to +36.9 at depth 3 (1.8 to 38.7), and the comparison is against ReAct, not chain of thought.
claim_before_audit: Decomposition gain in LLMs grows with task depth or length and vanishes or reverses on short tasks: GSM8K 2-step 74.53 vs 76.68 (worse), 5+ step 45.23 vs 39.07; TextCraft depth 2 26.9 to 78.2, depth 3 1.8 to 38.7; kth-letter concatenation stays near 100 while chain of thought falls with length.

claim: The weak link is the model's own decomposition, not the solving of the parts: a hand-made decomposition fixed nearly every failure (least-to-most), a perfect plan lifts HumanEval pass@1 from 60.3 to 74.4, and a stronger planner lifts a weak executor (LLaMA-2-70B 20.4 to 43.3 with a GPT-3.5 planner). Small models lose or stay flat when planning (code-cushman-001 34.0 direct vs 30.1 planned).
agent_test: Score plan quality separately (against a held-out solution or a code check) and correlate with final success; test whether plans from the best of several samples, chosen by code, raise results at equal tokens.
audit_note: Least-to-most (hand-made decomposition fixes nearly every GSM8K failure), Self-planning (60.3, 74.4, cushman 34.0 vs 30.1, davinci-002 plan lifts cushman to 44.9) and ADaPT (LLaMA-2-70B 20.4 to 43.3) all match.

claim: Plan-first prompting gives small gains over plain chain of thought (about 1 to 7 points; plain Plan-and-Solve +1.8 on GSM8K, 56.4 to 58.2, and PS+ +2.9; least-to-most +1.5 on GSM8K), mainly by cutting missing-step errors. Self-planning gains shrink with sampling: pass@10 is 76.3 vs 75.0 direct, against pass@1 60.3 vs 48.1. For reasoning models generic step-by-step prompting added almost nothing on GPQA Diamond (only o4-mini +5.6 points at one threshold) and cost 20 to 80% more time.
agent_test: Compare plan-first versus direct at pass@1 and at 5 samples with equal total tokens. Expect the gap to close at larger budgets.
audit_note: Plan-and-Solve numbers are mislabeled: in the PS paper's table 56.4/57.0/59.3 on GSM8K are Zero-shot-CoT/PoT/PS+; plain PS is 58.2 on GSM8K (+1.8 over CoT, not +0.6) and its six-dataset average is 72.9 (not 73.5, which is PoT). Least-to-most +1.5, self-planning pass@10 76.3 vs 75.0 and pass@1 60.3 vs 48.1, and the Meincke GPQA results (o4-mini +0.056 at one threshold, 20 to 80% more time) match; PS models were text-davinci-003, not strong models.
claim_before_audit: Plan-first prompting gives small gains over plain chain of thought on strong models (1 to 7 points; plain Plan-and-Solve +0.6 on GSM8K; least-to-most +1.5 on GSM8K), mainly by cutting missing-step errors. Self-planning gains shrink with sampling: pass@10 is 76.3 vs 75.0 direct, against pass@1 60.3 vs 48.1. Update: for reasoning models generic step-by-step prompting added almost nothing on GPQA Diamond (only o4-mini +5.6 points at one threshold) and cost 20 to 80% more time.

claim: Models answer every sub-question correctly yet fail the composed question: the compositionality gap is about 40% from 1B to 175B parameters, 42.9% for ChatGPT, 23.0% for GPT-4. Accuracy on multi-step composition decays toward zero as the computation graph deepens (3x3-digit multiplication: ChatGPT 55%, GPT-4 59%).
agent_test: Test the agent on composed items where sub-answers are right and recombination is wrong. Add a code recombination step and a final check on the composed answer (S8) and measure the gap closed.
audit_note: Press et al. (about 40% gap; 42.9% ChatGPT, 23.0% GPT-4) and Dziri et al. (3x3 multiplication ChatGPT 55%, GPT-4 59%) match; Press itself warns the GPT-4 figure may be invalid because the dataset predates GPT-4 and could be in its training data.

claim: More agents on a decomposed task help only when parts are independent: Finance (D=0.41) centralized +80.8%, PlanCraft (D=0.42) every variant loses (-39.1% to -70.0%), SWE-bench -2.1% to -14.9%. Aggregate effect -0.3% with CI -58.7% to +77.2%. Error amplification: independent 17.2x, decentralized 7.8x, hybrid 5.1x, centralized 4.4x. In Massoudi, the nine-agent decomposition made finer graphs (6 nodes) at about 650 s against 38.6 s and often crashed (Llama 0 of 5 completions).
agent_test: Keep a single-agent scaffold as baseline; split into parallel sub-agents only on items whose sub-tasks pass an independence check. Compare at equal tokens.
audit_note: All Finance/PlanCraft/SWE-bench/aggregate/error-amplification numbers match Kim et al.-style scaling paper; Massoudi 6 nodes, about 650 s vs 38.6 s match; in the scaling paper the error-amplification main effect was not significant after controls (p=0.658) and D is a domain-complexity score (Finance 0.41 vs PlanCraft 0.42), the paper attributes the contrast to parallelizable vs sequential subtasks.

claim: Answering sub-questions in separate contexts makes stated reasoning more faithful (answer change when a mistake is inserted 33.6% vs 9.6%; suggested-answer bias drop 9.2 vs 21.3 points) at an accuracy cost (average 81.8 vs 87.0; HotpotQA 83.0 vs 87.3).
agent_test: Use factored sub-question contexts only where faithfulness matters; measure the accuracy cost at equal tokens on a held-out set.

claim: Decomposition into function descriptions plus test-based selection among implementations beats equal-budget direct sampling: HumanEval at 128 samples direct 84.1% vs Parsel 93.9%; APPS pass@8x16 6% for direct-to-Python vs 25.5% for the full pipeline (100 problems). It needs tests to pick among implementations. Update: token-matched support is mixed. DISC beats best-of-N at equal tokens (APPS pass@10 error 0.50 to 0.475, LiveCodeBench 0.57 to 0.51), while PlanSearch needs about 10,000 tokens per problem to beat repeated sampling and trails it on o1-mini at low k.
agent_test: On code tasks with tests, compare decompose-then-test-select versus flat sampling at equal total samples.

claim: LLM-made function structures of engineering products score poorly in the one study with repeated runs: requirement coverage at most 20% over 60 runs, JSON validity 100%, flow edges often declared but not connected, physics errors even in the best 8-node graph. Small local models, one solar-filter case, no expert baseline. Two other LLM papers were seen only as abstracts (MCTS function decomposition with GPT-4o; Haddad and Seibel 2025). Update: the one LLM study with 50 products (Haddad and Seibel 2025) measured only rule validity, not match to expert structures: plain GPT-4o 16% error-free and 44% connected, with MCTS-FD 42% and 72%; human raters scored plain GPT-4o above the MCTS-FD variant (completeness 3.96 vs 3.53).
agent_test: Run a strong current model on 10 products that have expert Stone and Wood function structures; score sub-function recall and flow connectivity. This is the missing replication.

claim: Single-part function classification into 8 classes is near useless untuned (GPT-3.5 0.04, GPT-4o mini 0.20, GPT-4 Turbo 0.27) and reaches 0.89 test accuracy when tuned on 681 parts, falling to 0.63 with 6,130 (overfitting or imbalance suspected). This is labelling, not decomposition.
agent_test: Low priority for the schema.

claim: Decomposition can be posed as symbolic planning over a fixed function library (30 Roth functions as PDDL actions) and was solved in two worked examples. No benchmark or comparison with LLM or human results exists.
agent_test: Test whether a code-side planner over agent-proposed sub-goals beats the agent's free-text ordering at equal tokens.

claim: Evidence that function modelling helps designers is thin: the functional-basis authors report no measurement of benefit beyond a repeatability study, a 2017 review calls the empirical evidence for its benefits 'initial' (citing Kurfman, Caldwell, Srinivasan and Sen studies), and a Clemson dissertation abstract says there is little experimental evidence that function models help concept generation (the few experiments on it show no reliable gain).
agent_test: Treat O3 as unproven by default and require it to pay for itself at equal tokens (G7) in every test.
audit_note: Hirtz et al. (no measured benefit; repeatability study cited), Gericke and Eisenbart ('initial empirical evidence') and the Clemson abstract ('little experimental evidence' for ideation) match, but 'only repeatability and usage-frequency studies exist' is wider than the sources: Gericke cites further empirical studies (Caldwell 2011, Srinivasan 2012, Sen 2013) and the same dissertation and the Linsey and Booth experiments in this note are ideation experiments.
claim_before_audit: Evidence that function modelling helps designers is thin: the vocabulary authors give no measurement of benefit, a 2017 review calls empirical evidence initial, and a 2016 dissertation abstract says there is little experimental evidence on ideation. Only repeatability and usage-frequency studies exist.

claim: In the same industry sample where decomposition did not predict grade, use of a morphological matrix weakly did (total grade r=0.233, p=0.040; ideation r=0.293, p=0.009). Many tests, no correction, observational.
agent_test: Compare function-by-solution option tables (a combine step) with plain decomposition at equal tokens.

claim: Covariates swamped method in the dissection study: class level raised abstraction levels (3.5 sophomore, 4.17 junior, 4.84 senior), device order and fatigue lowered function counts, and 14 of 26 said they never learned decomposition. Device and time are confounded.
agent_test: None direct; for the agent, check order and context-length fatigue effects when decomposing in long runs.

claim: The best level of the vocabulary is disputed: modellers judged the tertiary level too coarse (121 repository models), while an information-content metric favoured the secondary level. Both come from one research group and one repository; numbers not read.
agent_test: Not directly testable. Use as a hint to try coarse versus fine sub-problem granularity.

claim: On a strong reasoning model, an explicit decomposition step at equal tokens has no clean test yet. Indirect evidence points both ways: generic step-by-step prompting gives about zero on reasoning models (GPQA Diamond, 25 trials per question), while unreplicated decompose-and-contract (Atom of Thoughts) reports +3.4 on AIME for o3-mini and +8.6 on LiveCodeBench, with cost not matched.
agent_test: Run o3-class and Claude-class models on 100 code-checked tasks: no step, forced decomposition, and decomposition at matched total tokens; report pass rate and tokens.

claim: LLMs can make rule-valid function graphs for 50 products, but the only study did not compare with expert Stone-and-Wood structures. GPT-4o with a check-and-refine tree search raised connected graphs from 44% to 72% and error-free graphs from 16% to 42%. Sub-function recall and flow accuracy against experts, and the effect of verb-object vocabulary, remain unmeasured.
agent_test: Build 10 or more expert function structures; score sub-function recall and flow edges for the agent with the Functional Basis vocabulary against free wording.

claim: Showing a function-level view of a prior answer is a lower-risk anchor for people than showing the answer. In 61 students, a function tree of a poor example gave no more fixation than no example and less than a sketch, but a sketch with the tree was worst. No LLM test of whether its own decomposition narrows its final answers exists.
agent_test: Generate answers with a decomposition first, with decomposition after a free first attempt, and with none; score answer diversity and constraint success.

claim: The gain from decomposition or planning in LLMs depends on plan quality and diversity, and token-matched gains are small. PlanSearch gains came from plan diversity and a correct sketch, but it needed about 10,000 tokens per problem to beat repeated sampling and often lowered pass@1. Plan-and-Act: an untrained planner failed to help trained executors, and replanning added +10.31 points over a static plan.
agent_test: Score plan quality against a held-out solution, correlate with final success, and compare against plain sampling at the same tokens.

claim: A half-enforced or superficial decomposition can be worse than none. In Atom of Thoughts, dropping the DAG-guided contraction hurt more than dropping decomposition; accuracy fell as depth and sub-question counts rose, and most problems split into 3 to 4 parts at depth 3. This fits the human Booth null if the diagrams were poor.
agent_test: Add a decomposition quality gate (cover the task, parts independent, each part checkable) and test with the gate on and off.

claim: The founding repeatability test (Kurfman et al. 2001, 2003) cannot be quantified: only abstracts were readable, saying the method is 'largely successful' with three experiments and mixed-skill participants. No participant counts or agreement percentages are available to us.
agent_test: Obtain the full text through a library before citing any repeatability figure.

claim: A per-task structure made once and reused is cheap compared with repeated sampling (Self-Discover: 1 call per instance plus 3 task-level calls against 10 to 40 calls for self-consistency or voting, GPT-4 and PaLM 2-L, 2023 models), but calls are not tokens and no equal-token test was run.
agent_test: Test one decomposition per task class, cached, against per-attempt decomposition at equal tokens.
